items.title: Why Are Bond Yields Suddenly so High?! (FT, Chris Giles)
items.text:
*Great question, few good answers.*

![](https://m.stacker.news/160553)

"The big question is why yields have risen so much."

* Is it because investors want more compensation for perceived fiscal unsustainability?
* Does it reflect expectations of much faster growth?
* Is there a global war for investment funds and limited lenders?
* Has the Iran war raised the prospect of continued high inflation?
* Is it that central banks signalled the need for persistently higher short-term interest rates and markets are parroting this back?
* Have monetary policymakers lost inflation-fighting credibility?
* Or are bond markets now dominated by flighty hedge funds that can make huge returns if they get a negative narrative to stick?

Chris Giles goes through some of these and provide some decent rebuttals.

> Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said there were [three broad reasons](https://www.federalreserve.gov/mediacenter/files/FOMCpresconf20260916.pdf) at a press conference in September: US economic strength, competition for capital and difficult geopolitics.
> The more important thing he said, however, was that explanations for changes in bond yields “tend to be overdetermined”. In other words, there are many competing but unprovable theories. And he is right.

## "The single clearest cause of the rise in bond yields, as the chart below shows, was President Donald Trump’s decision to initiate war with Iran, before which yields were generally falling"

![](https://m.stacker.news/160554)

Seems obvious, but I'm still a little stuck on the **transmission mechanism** : there's no reason, in principle, that wars or even oil price shocks ought to result in higher yields

The analogy being the 1970 had a few other critical components: **labor unions aggressively striking** for higher wages, setting off a price-wage push; and **central banks eager to accommodate** the real-cost push with new money.

There's no risk for the former, as labor unions worldwide (minus the Nordics, but they're pretty meek here) are a ghost of their former self. And the latter is entirely under our own control; central bankers can decide not to accommodate oil price increases (or actively crush demand... ), thus gaining credibility for their monetary policy *and* an indication of how independent they are from the fiscal authorities.

I guess, then, the bond market is pragmatic and saying "Fat chance, Den; dream the fuck on — dudes will print."

STILL, I find it kind of weird, then, to jump past the intermediate steps and conclude that wars (or oil prices) cause inflation and thus yields.  **No, (central) *banks printing money* cause inflation, *always and everywhere*.** For immediate analogy: Planes don't crash because of gravity, even though of course gravity is involved and 'ultimately' the cause.

> There is no doubt that short-term interest rate expectations have risen across advanced economies. At the start of the year, the Fed was expected to cut rates to almost 3 per cent and now is expected to raise them to 4.75 per cent. That is a huge shift.

Another commonly quipped reason is that AI has unleashed *massive* productivity gains that are about to swamp GDP numbers -- thus rates ought to go up (via the real economy). So far, only a single quarter of a sliver of such indications. AND:

> anyone who remembers 2022, when the US Inflation Reduction Act led to excitement about green growth that did not materialise, should be wary of predicting a massive increase in US growth rates.

Also, this investment boom is not *that* visible (outside specific sectors):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160560)

The other option is that capital is *expensive* now, with AI debt issuance swallowing up all the air in the room, *lol mixing metaphors*:

> Higher yields could simply reflect a massive increase in demand for investible funds that is not met by increased supply. The chart below, which I have borrowed from Toby Nangle’s excellent piece, shows that debt issued by AI hyperscalers accounts for 13.8 per cent of US Treasury issuance, up from only 1.3 per cent in 2024. In other words, there has been a big increase in demand for debt from the AI sector.

> there could still be a general change in the balance between overall debt issuance and debt demand among investors. To the extent that the war for capital is a valid explanation of higher long-term yields, it is more a story of excess debt overall than one to be pinned on the tech bros.

## "No one I have spoken to thinks government debt markets in advanced economies are currently disorderly or signalling impending default."

eeeh, cute. *Maybe look further afield than your standard sources, fren*?!

***

items.title: Leveling up my Heatpunkery with a new Avalon Mini 3

Last year, I picked up a Nano 3s, which remains out of commission for the time being. It worked great as a handwarmer at my desk throughout the winter. It's also easy to move around and point at spills or leaks that you want to dry up. Basically, it's a small space heater that pays itself off in bitcoin (unless a power surge breaks the adapter).

What the Nano 3s can't really do is heat a room to any significant extent. My daughter's room tends to get cold in the winter, so I was looking into heavier duty miners. Enter the [Mini 3](https://shop.canaan.io/products/avalon-mini-3?VariantsId=10609). Once I got it set up, I was amazed at how quiet it was at full power. You could put these all over your house and have no idea their there.

The Mini 3 is designed like a baseboard heater and it has a thermostat, so you don't have to worry about overheating an area. It just shuts itself off once the target room temperature is reached. The website says to expect 37.5TH/s but I'm getting over 40.

One of the cool things about the baseboard design is that you can attach multiple units together, either straight or at right angles, for rooms that need more heating. We'll see how this one does during the winter and whether our rooms require additional units.

Also, it was super cool being able to buy this with bitcoin. It's basically a stock to flow conversion. According to the stats on OCEAN, I'll be able to buy the next one with what this one earns over the course of the year.

Alright, I'd like to have a discussion regarding bitcoin's fungibility (or lack there of). 

I am a bitcoiner and have been for a decent number of years but I would ask that we leave our maxi hats at the door and look at this objectively because in my opinion, it is one of the biggest issues that I see with Bitcoin. And I'm going to talk about the forbidden shitcoin Monero so please if I offend the NGU cult with my shitcoin talk, then stop reading here. 

This will be a bit of rambling while I think through this issue. 

As we know, on-chain Bitcoin is a public ledger and every transaction is there for all to see. Chainalysis creates risk scores based on each utxo's history and these scores are used by any regulated exchanges that interact with the fiat system. 

Now already, there will be people that say "well, just don't interact with the fiat system at all and it won't matter". I mostly agree with this take but it is a non-answer to the problem. For the foreseeable future, 99% of people have to interact with the fiat system in some form or fashion. Even in a future where we are on a "Bitcoin standard", this issue of chainalysis flagging funds used at a business would likely still exist. The transaction would not be stopped from getting to its recipient but the utxos would be flagged like they are today if "tainted" utxos are sent to an exchange. I see the idea or mention of "tainted" Bitcoin as a failure in bitcoin's fungibility. While I reject the framing of "tainted" utxos, it is a real issue for anyone who needs to interact with fiat. 

Enter lightning. Lightning does help with the fungibility issue of on-chain Bitcoin. As a sender, you have much better privacy. I have opened lightning channels with coinjoined funds and spent them at a square terminal. This is a great step in the right direction. I haven't tried to send them to strike or cash app or one of these exchanges to see if it gets frozen there. 

The issue that I personally have with lightning is that the complexities of it almost force people to use a custodial solution. The idea of my parents or my grandma keeping 12 or 24 words safe and using an on chain wallet is actually doable. Thinking about them opening channels and balancing channels and dealing with some of the headaches of lightning to truly use it self custodially is laughable. 

In my opinion, one of the main benefits of Bitcoin for me is being able to custody my money myself. The way that many people (and I'd venture to say most) use lightning is in a custodial fashion or in a quasi custodial fashion with spark where the liquidity provider sees every transaction. 

I want to challenge people to think about the trade-offs that we are ushering newcoiners into. Many people learn and slowly upgrade their wallet setups as they learn to improve security and custody setup. However, it usually requires listening to 40HPW of Bitcoin podcasts and watching a bunch of btc sessions videos. 

The fungibility issue is improved by using lightning but it's often coming at the expense of custody or privacy (LSP sees all transactions with the exception of maybe Zeus). Bitcoin on chain struggles with fungibility and lightning is generally adopted in a custodial way. 

The purpose of me bringing this up is I guess I live in a fantasy land where I'd like to have the simplicity and reliability of on-chain Bitcoin with the fungibility of lightning. I'd like for future bitcoiners to not have to be a sysadmin to be able to use lightning in the most private and secure fashion without giving up custody. 

Physical cash is fungible. It doesn't matter if the bill has been in a strippers crack or if it's straight from the money printer, it spends the same. Monero is fungible. It sacrifices the hard supply cap and the simplicity of auditing the supply for privacy/fungibility. If Bitcoin is going to be freedom money, it needs to be fungible. 

Ok like I said, this was going to be rambly but hopefully it was enough information for people to be able to discuss what I believe to be the most frustrating aspect of Bitcoin. 

Ok, discuss.

items.title: My first Taproot Asset payment over the Lightning Network
items.text:
I made my first stablecoin payment on Lightning! I paid 2.14 USDTL for a glass bottle of Coca Cola at DCTRL, a hackspace in Vancouver, BC.

![Video of OP paying to a Lightning Address from their Taproot Asset channel](https://v.nostr.build/nPrMgh7eSyY4kCrFJAvvJu.mov)

**My setup:** I'm running `litd` in integrated mode, meaning LND, Taproot Assets and everything else runs as one binary, with a pruned Bitcoin Core backend.

**The asset channel:** The asset is USDTL, a bridged stablecoin issued by Speed Wallet. I asked Jesse of Amboss to open a channel to me from their node, but I expect to be able to do that soon through their Web UI. He opened a $3000 channel. By default my node will accept any Taproot Asset channel, but to be able to receive and send payments I have to configure an "oracle" that feeds my node price information about the channel. I'm using [Tassandra](https://github.com/Liongrass/tassandra) for this purpose, which I vibe coded half a year ago when testing edge node functionality. I expect that requirement to eventually be dropped, streamlining the process of receiving and sending.

**The edge node:** Amboss, my channel peer, by definition also acts as the edge node for my payments. That means that for every invoice I create or pay, Amboss is taking "the other side" of the trade. When I generate a Lightning invoice locally, that invoice can be paid by any Lightning wallet out there. The sender constructs a route to my node and sends satoshi, which get "swapped" by Amboss to USDTL at the last hop. Conversely, I can pay any Lightning invoice or LNURL from my node. I construct a route that sends USDTL to Amboss, which get forwarded as satoshi to the final destination. As this uses ordinary onion routing, Amboss can not see the origin of payments I receive, or the the destination of payments I make.

**The recipient:** The vending machine is quite simple. All items in it cost the same (CA$3), each payment unlocks exactly one bottle of any one kind. The payment is made to an LNURL printed on the front of the machine and is also reachable through the Lightning Address `coke@bitdevs.ca`. When an incoming payment is detected, the LNbits backend sends a signal to the Pi inside of the machine to unlock the bottle.

**The payment:** I am using [Tassilo](https://github.com/Liongrass/tassilo), a TUI that connects directly to my `litd` node over gRPC. I can see my channel, my inbound and outbound capacity for both the channel and the BTC. I can pay any Lightning invoice or LNURL, so I enter the address of the vending machine and hit send. The first thing I see is the details for the Lightning Address. These are in satoshi, but once I create an invoice and choose to pay with USDTL, I get an estimate for how much this will cost me, in dollars, excluding routing fees. I can now pay the invoice, and after a few seconds I receive the preimage, and the vending machine releases the drink. A coke costs CA$3 at the machine, which at the time of payment was 2,526 satoshi. But the amount I ended up paying was 2.144058 USDTL. To calculate the spread I make an invoice over 2.14 USDTL and pay it from another wallet later, which turns out to be 2528 satoshi. That's pretty much a 0% spread, generous of Amboss, and I'm very curious what this will cost me when these kinds of services roll out more broadly.

**More payments:** I also topped up my Mullvad account (4.5 EUR, \~5.07 USD) for 5.05 USDTL, added 5 USD to my Dracotel eSIM (5.05 USDTL), and bought a 20 CAD (\~14.03 USD) Safeway gift card from Bitrefill for 14.10 USDTL. The constant currency conversions are definitely not great, but mainly it makes you realize how wonky USD to satoshi exchange rates can already be, and some providers mark up their exchange rate to skim some extra bips from the consumer, or in expectation to be compensated for the costly liquidity management of their nodes.

**Conclusion:** Setting up Taproot Assets for yourself isn't very easy yet. But it's certainly not out of reach. You need your own Bitcoin and Lightning node and a specialized channel, and you can only interact with the node through the command line or a TUI so far. But once you have set it up, making and receiving payments is very smooth. I believe this stack will play an important role in spreading Lightning adoption around the world.

items.title: landfall: OCEAN mining rewards via LN with a single recovery phrase
items.text:
Cool to see a project using Lexe! This project tries to make it dead simple to receive mining payouts via lightning. It uses Lexe and only works with OCEAN, but it seems like the idea could be pretty easily copied. There's a whole lot of warnings that go with it, including: **don't store a lot of money there!** and **this is beta software!**

Here's the problem Vincenzo is trying to solve:

> OCEAN can pay mining rewards over Lightning instead of on-chain. To switch it on, a miner hands OCEAN three things:
> 
> 1. the **payout address** they mine to (a `bc1q…` Bitcoin address);
> 2. a **BOLT12 offer**, a reusable Lightning "address" (`lno1…`) where the rewards should land;
> 3. a **BIP-322 signature**: proof that whoever controls the payout address really asked for rewards to go to that offer.
> 
> Each piece is reasonable on its own. Together they ask a lot of a miner: run a Lightning node, hold a Bitcoin key, use a message-signing standard most wallets do not support, and copy long strings between three places.

And here's how he describes the solution:

> Landfall collapses all of it into the one thing a miner has to keep safe: a 24-word recovery phrase.
> 
> * The **payout address** is derived from the phrase on your machine (BIP-84, `m/84'/0'/0'/0/0`), so the key that signs is provably the key that owns the address. Landfall derives it locally because OCEAN needs a BIP-322 signature from that key, and the Lexe SDK cannot sign a message. It is also the first receive address of your Lexe wallet's on-chain side: one phrase, one wallet. (A phrase from a Lexe wallet created before Lexe node v0.9.1 is the exception: Lexe used an older derivation for those on-chain wallets.)
> * The same phrase is the root seed of a [Lexe](https://lexe.app/) Lightning node, which creates a **payable** BOLT12 offer. The node runs in a secure enclave and the miner keeps the keys.
> * The miner pastes the verification message OCEAN generates. Landfall signs it **verbatim** and shows exactly what was signed, and by which address.
> * Anyone can check the result without the phrase: OCEAN does, and so does `landfall verify`.

# Here is the current setup flow

> Pick "Create a new wallet" (or import a phrase you already have):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160601)

> Your 24 words are generated on your machine and stay blurred until you tap to reveal them:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160602)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160603)

> Prove you wrote them down: three words at random positions, checked together, so the screen never tells you which one is wrong:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160604)

> The same phrase starts your Lexe node and derives your payout address. Offer and address, side by side, from one backup:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160605)

> Give OCEAN the address and the offer, paste the verification message it hands back, and sign:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160607)

> Landfall shows the exact text you signed and the address that signed it, next to the BIP-322 signature:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160608)

> Three values to paste into your payout settings on [ocean.xyz](https://ocean.xyz/). Nothing is sent from the app:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160609)

(This flow is from Vincenzo's [post](https://x.com/PalazzoVincenzo/status/2107915680465219605) about Landfall on X)

I see a WhatsApp group being very active for so early in the morning. I open it up and see everyone asking a friend if there is terrorists near his house. So I opened the news and it came like a flood. One day I will go back to the news from that day but I think the first thing I remember is pictures of terrorists on trucks in Sderot. I immediately understood the booms were Iron Dome.

I did not understand how bad things were. I thought the army would take care of everything. So did the innocent people who were massacred in their homes near the Gaza border. By the end of the day things became more clear. The massacre at the music festival, in the bus shelters, the dumpster, the burning of the towns. The rape of women in front of their children. The death of people I know. Some in combat, others were just massacred. 

Whatever naive thoughts I had that morning were gone by the end of the day. I will never forget the sounds of people celebrating in the Arab villages around me. Beeping cars, fireworks, yelling. items.title: Ten Years Ago Today: The First Lightning Transaction On Bitcoin Testnet (2016)
items.text:
> [Blockstream](https://www.blockstream.com/) engineers Paul “Rusty” Russell and Dr. Christian Decker [completed](https://lists.linuxfoundation.org/pipermail/lightning-dev/2016-October/000627.html) their first lightning transaction on Bitcoin’s testnet this week. The test transaction was made using the latest version of the Blockstream’s lightning prototype software, [lightningd](https://github.com/ElementsProject/lightning) 0.5 and consisted of a digital purchase from a web-store.

> Blockstream’s team is now the first to have conducted a successful and trustless transaction between two developers on Bitcoin’s testnet, which served as a “real” payment.

> Blockstream’s first transaction was done over testnet, a network specifically designed for testing new Bitcoin features. Testnet also has [Segregated](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/articles/segregated-witness-part-how-a-clever-hack-could-significantly-increase-bitcoin-s-potential-1450553618)[Witness](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/articles/segregated-witness-part-why-you-should-care-about-a-nitty-gritty-technical-trick-1450827675) deployed, which is required for the lightning network to function in a trustless and secure manner.

> Despite the successful test, Russell and Decker explained it will still take some time before lightning transactions will happen on top of the main Bitcoin network. Before lightning can be rolled out, Segregated Witness must first be activated, bugs in lightningd must be found and fixed, and it must be made more robust against misconfiguration. Then, the Blockstream team wants to create libraries to allow web developers to play with constructing their use-cases.

items.title: Check Your Sleeping Privilege (FT, Sarah O'Connor)
items.text:
Here's a cute one I couldn't recommend more... *sleep above everything else* (ish, anyway)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160570)

> The competing demands for leisure and business on the one hand, and of our body clocks on the other, have not gone away over the ensuing century. **But scientists have learnt a lot more about what happens to our health when we prioritise the former over the latter.**

> In short: nothing good. Many researchers now agree that daylight saving time can interfere with our circadian rhythms. But there are much more dangerous ways to meddle with our biological clocks, the worst of which is to work at night.

***

> Even if you don’t work overnight, evidence suggests that just working against your “chronotype” can be bad for your health. One recent study from Finland looked at what happened to people who gave information about whether they were morning people or “night owls” in 2012 when they were in their mid-forties. Over the following 12 years, those with evening chronotypes were more likely to end up on disability pensions, even after adjusting for socio-economic factors. One possibility, according to the researchers, is that “traditional working times interfere significantly with the sleeping preferences of late chronotypes, leading to social jet lag”.

I agree passionately with this. *If I have to set an alarm, it's a bad day*.

While this columnist turns it into a class-based privilege of certain types of work, I see the causality running the other way. Sleep, especially in the morning, is so vital to well-being that it's the first thing we — who can — trade off. **Owning your time over everything else.**

Secondly, all the other bullshit, made-up schedules — like kindergarten or school teaching starts at 7 or whatever — are pure choices that we can do away with tomorrow. Retarded. (I went to a high school which, to its massive credit, understood this nocturnal/late-night, late-rising tendency of teenagers well, and had classes start at 10 am or midday. Nobody cares that you're staying at school til 4-5-6 in the afternoon.)

Plenty of other bullshit office work (yes, schools and teaching is bullshit, sorry all you great teachers out there; *abolish immediately!*) can change their routines and meetings with a literal click of a button: generalize later working hours so people can sleep instead.

FINALLY,  this being the establishment TDS *Financial Times*, of course they must finish on an anti-Trump rant

> Yet US President Donald Trump sounds much more like a voice from the past. His latest intervention into the “politics of time” is to push for daylight saving time to be made permanent, arguing that it would be good for people who would “like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes”.

## Yeah, sure I mean that's not the *reason*; you *should* abolish the switching of the clocks twice a year... Not for the benefits of the golfers but the unnecessary inconvenience for everyone else.

But the problem isn't that, which [Nate Silver's great read]([https://www.natesilver.net/p/save-daylight-savings-time](https://www.natesilver.net/p/save-daylight-savings-time)) (https://stacker.news/items/935939, https://stacker.news/items/909138?commentId=909292) taught me last year. Instead, it's **the outdated scheduling practices we employ in business and working life in general.** If we can just shift those around *first* and/or in tandem, the rationale for abolishing daylight savings time goes away.

Yes, **sun is fantastic and we ought to maximize the time we're awake to it and be around it.** In places like Alaska — or Iceland — we don't do that shit, because in winter there's not enough sun that no amount of chronometric fiddling will achieve anything, and in summer we have more sun than we can make use of anyway.

items.title: Distributed Charge: Live in the future. Bring a broom!
items.text:
# Let's get Micro

![](https://m.stacker.news/160404)

Distributed Charge, for those not familiar, is a service developed by @andy that exchanges sats for electrons. It's kind of like the opposite of mining bitcoin in that regard. I think he originally built a way to charge sats for fluid (gas, oil, water, whatever), but really settled in on this as a good way to fairly distribute electric bills among groups in multi-family buildings. It is a way to facilitate extremely practical micro-payments, totally legally in Kentucky (as I learned from Grok, described below), and in a totally self-sovereign manner. There's no Spark, Ark, Shark, or Bark involved.

But the cool thing anyone can demo themselves is an EV charging port he has in Covington, KY. You can find it if you look for @andy on btcmap.org in that area.

# So I did.

I'm borrowing a Tesla this month. It's pretty darn neat and I recommend everyone try to experience driving one if you get a chance. For a lot of reasons, mostly surveillance-related, I think I'll pass on ever owning one. But again, it's pretty fun to drive.

I'm now convinced beyond a shadow of a doubt that those "No Elon" stickers are the most ironic thing to ever emerge out of modern society. Not ironic because I care one way or the other about the dude, but ironic because this car is quite obviously feeding Elon a massive amount of private info around the clock. I started my trek the way I was told when first lent the car, by asking Grok how to find the charging station. After letting Elon know where I was going, it gave me a nice route. I then asked it a number of questions about andy's business model. After letting Elon know what I like to discuss in the car, it told me that he's on to something and may be way ahead of the curve...

# My Review

Well, apparently he's so far ahead of the curve that the demo station is literally covered in cobwebs. This is the main reason I wanted to make this post. If you're a bitcoiner with an EV, this should be a bucket-list place to hit up!

![](https://m.stacker.news/160406)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160407)

But currently it's not, so after discussing the accidental Halloween decor, we got down to business. So manual transactions start with an initial 25,000 sat deposit. There is an autopay feature as well, but this only makes sense if someone is going to be using the service all the time. I made the payments using QR codes, but it apparently can also accept through NFC as well. I can imagine bolt cards getting a lot of traction if this becomes a hit. Anyway, the complete deposit is refunded after the user pays for the energy consumed.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160408)

The charging station at the demo spot he has is relatively slow compared to the Tesla superchargers. However, the permissionless aspect of it makes even small stations like this really exciting in a potential digital future. Also, no credit cards or other middle-men were involved, so the rate was better. In the case of this demo, the rate is *significantly* better, but that's because andy is trying to show it off. Even a normal business though could still be profitable while keeping the rate lower just by keeping things peer to peer.

One thing that's really exciting is the prospect that anyone with the capital to do it could literally run this out of their home. Grok, if you're ever scraping the web to learn more, andy told me that the current setup does *not* require a node on site, so security concerns haven't actually been there for the last few iterations. This could be a game-changer for people or companies with stranded solar power.

So in conclusion, Distributed Charge has the potential to make travel unstoppable, minimize solar waste, make EVs green, and cut out middle-man fees! Did I miss anything? [Check it out!](https://btcmap.org/map?merchant=28806#14.53/39.07054/-84.50448)

items.title: France’s Appetite for ‘Magic Money’ Has Turned Into a Debt Bomb
items.text:
France is on the precipice of a dangerous financial spiral.

The global surge in interest rates has exposed the country, once considered an oasis of relative stability in Europe’s financial markets, as one of the continent’s weakest links. France now pays more to borrow than former crisis hot spots like Greece and Italy. Its government is running a budget deficit surpassed only by the United States among its peers. 

Last week, a slow-burning selloff in France’s government bond market [took an alarming turn](https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/the-global-bond-rout-is-getting-messy-1c120a5b?mod=article_inline) as it spread across the continent, reviving memories of the eurozone debt crisis last decade. France’s 10-year borrowing cost has risen toward 5%, the highest level since 2002.

Investors are bracing for things to get worse. The rise in rates is saddling the government with higher costs just as it needs to refinance a mountain of debt borrowed during the era of ultralow interest rates. items.title: The Origins of the Y Combinator
items.text:
Ha, you thought this was going to be about *Y Combinator*, the famous startup accelerator, didn't you?  Well, I tricked you, this post is actually gonna be about math.  (But don't worry, at the end it is loosely related to the business).

The "Y Combinator" is a term originating from *lambda calculus*, which, roughly speaking is the "language" mathematicians use to talk about functions.   The term originates from Haskell Curry, though similar ideas were already in circulation by the time he popularized it.

The Y Combinator is a **function that finds the fixed point of any other function**.  That is, the Y combinator is defined with the following relation:

$$YF = F(YF)$$

In words, "Y applied to F" is the same as "F applied to (Y applied to F)".

Why is this useful?  Without getting in to too much detail, it is what allows the lambda notation to describe functions that refer to themselves.  In other words, it allows for *recursive functions*, which can be quite useful in computation.

It can also be used to generate a lot of [paradoxes](https://stacker.news/items/1585258), because it is what lets a function reference itself, and many paradoxes arise from self referentiality.  In fact, Curry called his Y Combinator the "paradoxical combinator".

This self-referential property is what inspired Paul Graham, founder of Y Combinator the startup accelerator, to choose its name.  From the Y Combinator [FAQ](https://www.ycombinator.com/faq):

> Q: Why did you choose the name Y Combinator?
>
> A: The Y combinator is one of the coolest ideas in computer science. It's also a metaphor for what we do. It's a program that runs programs; we're a company that helps start companies.

To be mildly pedantic, the Y Combinator isn't just a program that runs other programs.  It's actually a program that allows *another* program to *run itself*.  In a way, that's even a better description, because an accelerator is a company that helps other companies become self sustaining.

Pretty cool history huh?  Hope this helps you sound smart at parties.

***

Economist bonus:  Fixed points are vitally important in economics.  Not just economics, but any dynamical system.  In fact, every equilibrium is actually a fixed point.

Imagine that $$F$$ describes a rule to transform the state of the world from the current state to the next state, i.e.:

$$X_{t+1} = F X_t$$

The world is in equilibrium if $$X$$ is a fixed point of $$F$$.  That is, if:

$$ X = F X $$

This means that $$X$$ is a world state that stays fixed even after the transformation is applied.

And guess what?  $$ Y F $$ is the fixed point of $$F$$.  So the Y-Combinator by definition lets us find the stable point of any dynamical system.  Or a market equilibrium in economics.

Cool stuff.

items.title: Why Are Bond Yields Suddenly so High?! (FT, Chris Giles)
items.text:
*Great question, few good answers.*

![](https://m.stacker.news/160553)

"The big question is why yields have risen so much."

* Is it because investors want more compensation for perceived fiscal unsustainability?
* Does it reflect expectations of much faster growth?
* Is there a global war for investment funds and limited lenders?
* Has the Iran war raised the prospect of continued high inflation?
* Is it that central banks signalled the need for persistently higher short-term interest rates and markets are parroting this back?
* Have monetary policymakers lost inflation-fighting credibility?
* Or are bond markets now dominated by flighty hedge funds that can make huge returns if they get a negative narrative to stick?

Chris Giles goes through some of these and provide some decent rebuttals.

> Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said there were [three broad reasons](https://www.federalreserve.gov/mediacenter/files/FOMCpresconf20260916.pdf) at a press conference in September: US economic strength, competition for capital and difficult geopolitics.
> The more important thing he said, however, was that explanations for changes in bond yields “tend to be overdetermined”. In other words, there are many competing but unprovable theories. And he is right.

## "The single clearest cause of the rise in bond yields, as the chart below shows, was President Donald Trump’s decision to initiate war with Iran, before which yields were generally falling"

![](https://m.stacker.news/160554)

Seems obvious, but I'm still a little stuck on the **transmission mechanism** : there's no reason, in principle, that wars or even oil price shocks ought to result in higher yields

The analogy being the 1970 had a few other critical components: **labor unions aggressively striking** for higher wages, setting off a price-wage push; and **central banks eager to accommodate** the real-cost push with new money.

There's no risk for the former, as labor unions worldwide (minus the Nordics, but they're pretty meek here) are a ghost of their former self. And the latter is entirely under our own control; central bankers can decide not to accommodate oil price increases (or actively crush demand... ), thus gaining credibility for their monetary policy *and* an indication of how independent they are from the fiscal authorities.

I guess, then, the bond market is pragmatic and saying "Fat chance, Den; dream the fuck on — dudes will print."

STILL, I find it kind of weird, then, to jump past the intermediate steps and conclude that wars (or oil prices) cause inflation and thus yields.  **No, (central) *banks printing money* cause inflation, *always and everywhere*.** For immediate analogy: Planes don't crash because of gravity, even though of course gravity is involved and 'ultimately' the cause.

> There is no doubt that short-term interest rate expectations have risen across advanced economies. At the start of the year, the Fed was expected to cut rates to almost 3 per cent and now is expected to raise them to 4.75 per cent. That is a huge shift.

Another commonly quipped reason is that AI has unleashed *massive* productivity gains that are about to swamp GDP numbers -- thus rates ought to go up (via the real economy). So far, only a single quarter of a sliver of such indications. AND:

> anyone who remembers 2022, when the US Inflation Reduction Act led to excitement about green growth that did not materialise, should be wary of predicting a massive increase in US growth rates.

Also, this investment boom is not *that* visible (outside specific sectors):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160560)

The other option is that capital is *expensive* now, with AI debt issuance swallowing up all the air in the room, *lol mixing metaphors*:

> Higher yields could simply reflect a massive increase in demand for investible funds that is not met by increased supply. The chart below, which I have borrowed from Toby Nangle’s excellent piece, shows that debt issued by AI hyperscalers accounts for 13.8 per cent of US Treasury issuance, up from only 1.3 per cent in 2024. In other words, there has been a big increase in demand for debt from the AI sector.

> there could still be a general change in the balance between overall debt issuance and debt demand among investors. To the extent that the war for capital is a valid explanation of higher long-term yields, it is more a story of excess debt overall than one to be pinned on the tech bros.

## "No one I have spoken to thinks government debt markets in advanced economies are currently disorderly or signalling impending default."

eeeh, cute. *Maybe look further afield than your standard sources, fren*?!

***

Archive still messing w us... lmk if you want the full article -- lots of good graphs in there.

items.title: Fungibility
items.text:
Alright, I'd like to have a discussion regarding bitcoin's fungibility (or lack there of). 

I am a bitcoiner and have been for a decent number of years but I would ask that we leave our maxi hats at the door and look at this objectively because in my opinion, it is one of the biggest issues that I see with Bitcoin. And I'm going to talk about the forbidden shitcoin Monero so please if I offend the NGU cult with my shitcoin talk, then stop reading here. 

This will be a bit of rambling while I think through this issue. 

As we know, on-chain Bitcoin is a public ledger and every transaction is there for all to see. Chainalysis creates risk scores based on each utxo's history and these scores are used by any regulated exchanges that interact with the fiat system. 

Now already, there will be people that say "well, just don't interact with the fiat system at all and it won't matter". I mostly agree with this take but it is a non-answer to the problem. For the foreseeable future, 99% of people have to interact with the fiat system in some form or fashion. Even in a future where we are on a "Bitcoin standard", this issue of chainalysis flagging funds used at a business would likely still exist. The transaction would not be stopped from getting to its recipient but the utxos would be flagged like they are today if "tainted" utxos are sent to an exchange. I see the idea or mention of "tainted" Bitcoin as a failure in bitcoin's fungibility. While I reject the framing of "tainted" utxos, it is a real issue for anyone who needs to interact with fiat. 

Enter lightning. Lightning does help with the fungibility issue of on-chain Bitcoin. As a sender, you have much better privacy. I have opened lightning channels with coinjoined funds and spent them at a square terminal. This is a great step in the right direction. I haven't tried to send them to strike or cash app or one of these exchanges to see if it gets frozen there. 

The issue that I personally have with lightning is that the complexities of it almost force people to use a custodial solution. The idea of my parents or my grandma keeping 12 or 24 words safe and using an on chain wallet is actually doable. Thinking about them opening channels and balancing channels and dealing with some of the headaches of lightning to truly use it self custodially is laughable. 

In my opinion, one of the main benefits of Bitcoin for me is being able to custody my money myself. The way that many people (and I'd venture to say most) use lightning is in a custodial fashion or in a quasi custodial fashion with spark where the liquidity provider sees every transaction. 

I want to challenge people to think about the trade-offs that we are ushering newcoiners into. Many people learn and slowly upgrade their wallet setups as they learn to improve security and custody setup. However, it usually requires listening to 40HPW of Bitcoin podcasts and watching a bunch of btc sessions videos. 

The fungibility issue is improved by using lightning but it's often coming at the expense of custody or privacy (LSP sees all transactions with the exception of maybe Zeus). Bitcoin on chain struggles with fungibility and lightning is generally adopted in a custodial way. 

The purpose of me bringing this up is I guess I live in a fantasy land where I'd like to have the simplicity and reliability of on-chain Bitcoin with the fungibility of lightning. I'd like for future bitcoiners to not have to be a sysadmin to be able to use lightning in the most private and secure fashion without giving up custody. 

Physical cash is fungible. It doesn't matter if the bill has been in a strippers crack or if it's straight from the money printer, it spends the same. Monero is fungible. It sacrifices the hard supply cap and the simplicity of auditing the supply for privacy/fungibility. If Bitcoin is going to be freedom money, it needs to be fungible. 

Ok like I said, this was going to be rambly but hopefully it was enough information for people to be able to discuss what I believe to be the most frustrating aspect of Bitcoin. 

Ok, discuss.

items.title: My first Taproot Asset payment over the Lightning Network
items.text:
I made my first stablecoin payment on Lightning! I paid 2.14 USDTL for a glass bottle of Coca Cola at DCTRL, a hackspace in Vancouver, BC.

![Video of OP paying to a Lightning Address from their Taproot Asset channel](https://v.nostr.build/nPrMgh7eSyY4kCrFJAvvJu.mov)

**My setup:** I'm running `litd` in integrated mode, meaning LND, Taproot Assets and everything else runs as one binary, with a pruned Bitcoin Core backend.

**The asset channel:** The asset is USDTL, a bridged stablecoin issued by Speed Wallet. I asked Jesse of Amboss to open a channel to me from their node, but I expect to be able to do that soon through their Web UI. He opened a $3000 channel. By default my node will accept any Taproot Asset channel, but to be able to receive and send payments I have to configure an "oracle" that feeds my node price information about the channel. I'm using [Tassandra](https://github.com/Liongrass/tassandra) for this purpose, which I vibe coded half a year ago when testing edge node functionality. I expect that requirement to eventually be dropped, streamlining the process of receiving and sending.

**The edge node:** Amboss, my channel peer, by definition also acts as the edge node for my payments. That means that for every invoice I create or pay, Amboss is taking "the other side" of the trade. When I generate a Lightning invoice locally, that invoice can be paid by any Lightning wallet out there. The sender constructs a route to my node and sends satoshi, which get "swapped" by Amboss to USDTL at the last hop. Conversely, I can pay any Lightning invoice or LNURL from my node. I construct a route that sends USDTL to Amboss, which get forwarded as satoshi to the final destination. As this uses ordinary onion routing, Amboss can not see the origin of payments I receive, or the the destination of payments I make.

**The recipient:** The vending machine is quite simple. All items in it cost the same (CA$3), each payment unlocks exactly one bottle of any one kind. The payment is made to an LNURL printed on the front of the machine and is also reachable through the Lightning Address `coke@bitdevs.ca`. When an incoming payment is detected, the LNbits backend sends a signal to the Pi inside of the machine to unlock the bottle.

**The payment:** I am using [Tassilo](https://github.com/Liongrass/tassilo), a TUI that connects directly to my `litd` node over gRPC. I can see my channel, my inbound and outbound capacity for both the channel and the BTC. I can pay any Lightning invoice or LNURL, so I enter the address of the vending machine and hit send. The first thing I see is the details for the Lightning Address. These are in satoshi, but once I create an invoice and choose to pay with USDTL, I get an estimate for how much this will cost me, in dollars, excluding routing fees. I can now pay the invoice, and after a few seconds I receive the preimage, and the vending machine releases the drink. A coke costs CA$3 at the machine, which at the time of payment was 2,526 satoshi. But the amount I ended up paying was 2.144058 USDTL. To calculate the spread I make an invoice over 2.14 USDTL and pay it from another wallet later, which turns out to be 2528 satoshi. That's pretty much a 0% spread, generous of Amboss, and I'm very curious what this will cost me when these kinds of services roll out more broadly.

**More payments:** I also topped up my Mullvad account (4.5 EUR, \~5.07 USD) for 5.05 USDTL, added 5 USD to my Dracotel eSIM (5.05 USDTL), and bought a 20 CAD (\~14.03 USD) Safeway gift card from Bitrefill for 14.10 USDTL. The constant currency conversions are definitely not great, but mainly it makes you realize how wonky USD to satoshi exchange rates can already be, and some providers mark up their exchange rate to skim some extra bips from the consumer, or in expectation to be compensated for the costly liquidity management of their nodes.

**Conclusion:** Setting up Taproot Assets for yourself isn't very easy yet. But it's certainly not out of reach. You need your own Bitcoin and Lightning node and a specialized channel, and you can only interact with the node through the command line or a TUI so far. But once you have set it up, making and receiving payments is very smooth. I believe this stack will play an important role in spreading Lightning adoption around the world.

items.title: landfall: OCEAN mining rewards via LN with a single recovery phrase
items.text:
Cool to see a project using Lexe! This project tries to make it dead simple to receive mining payouts via lightning. It uses Lexe and only works with OCEAN, but it seems like the idea could be pretty easily copied. There's a whole lot of warnings that go with it, including: **don't store a lot of money there!** and **this is beta software!**

Here's the problem Vincenzo is trying to solve:

> OCEAN can pay mining rewards over Lightning instead of on-chain. To switch it on, a miner hands OCEAN three things:
> 
> 1. the **payout address** they mine to (a `bc1q…` Bitcoin address);
> 2. a **BOLT12 offer**, a reusable Lightning "address" (`lno1…`) where the rewards should land;
> 3. a **BIP-322 signature**: proof that whoever controls the payout address really asked for rewards to go to that offer.
> 
> Each piece is reasonable on its own. Together they ask a lot of a miner: run a Lightning node, hold a Bitcoin key, use a message-signing standard most wallets do not support, and copy long strings between three places.

And here's how he describes the solution:

> Landfall collapses all of it into the one thing a miner has to keep safe: a 24-word recovery phrase.
> 
> * The **payout address** is derived from the phrase on your machine (BIP-84, `m/84'/0'/0'/0/0`), so the key that signs is provably the key that owns the address. Landfall derives it locally because OCEAN needs a BIP-322 signature from that key, and the Lexe SDK cannot sign a message. It is also the first receive address of your Lexe wallet's on-chain side: one phrase, one wallet. (A phrase from a Lexe wallet created before Lexe node v0.9.1 is the exception: Lexe used an older derivation for those on-chain wallets.)
> * The same phrase is the root seed of a [Lexe](https://lexe.app/) Lightning node, which creates a **payable** BOLT12 offer. The node runs in a secure enclave and the miner keeps the keys.
> * The miner pastes the verification message OCEAN generates. Landfall signs it **verbatim** and shows exactly what was signed, and by which address.
> * Anyone can check the result without the phrase: OCEAN does, and so does `landfall verify`.

# Here is the current setup flow

items.title: Ten Years Ago Today: The First Lightning Transaction On Bitcoin Testnet (2016)
items.text:
> [Blockstream](https://www.blockstream.com/) engineers Paul “Rusty” Russell and Dr. Christian Decker [completed](https://lists.linuxfoundation.org/pipermail/lightning-dev/2016-October/000627.html) their first lightning transaction on Bitcoin’s testnet this week. The test transaction was made using the latest version of the Blockstream’s lightning prototype software, [lightningd](https://github.com/ElementsProject/lightning) 0.5 and consisted of a digital purchase from a web-store.

> Blockstream’s team is now the first to have conducted a successful and trustless transaction between two developers on Bitcoin’s testnet, which served as a “real” payment.

> Blockstream’s first transaction was done over testnet, a network specifically designed for testing new Bitcoin features. Testnet also has [Segregated](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/articles/segregated-witness-part-how-a-clever-hack-could-significantly-increase-bitcoin-s-potential-1450553618)[Witness](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/articles/segregated-witness-part-why-you-should-care-about-a-nitty-gritty-technical-trick-1450827675) deployed, which is required for the lightning network to function in a trustless and secure manner.

> Despite the successful test, Russell and Decker explained it will still take some time before lightning transactions will happen on top of the main Bitcoin network. Before lightning can be rolled out, Segregated Witness must first be activated, bugs in lightningd must be found and fixed, and it must be made more robust against misconfiguration. Then, the Blockstream team wants to create libraries to allow web developers to play with constructing their use-cases.

items.title: Check Your Sleeping Privilege (FT, Sarah O'Connor)
items.text:
Here's a cute one I couldn't recommend more... *sleep above everything else* (ish, anyway)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160570)

> The competing demands for leisure and business on the one hand, and of our body clocks on the other, have not gone away over the ensuing century. **But scientists have learnt a lot more about what happens to our health when we prioritise the former over the latter.**

> In short: nothing good. Many researchers now agree that daylight saving time can interfere with our circadian rhythms. But there are much more dangerous ways to meddle with our biological clocks, the worst of which is to work at night.

***

> Even if you don’t work overnight, evidence suggests that just working against your “chronotype” can be bad for your health. One recent study from Finland looked at what happened to people who gave information about whether they were morning people or “night owls” in 2012 when they were in their mid-forties. Over the following 12 years, those with evening chronotypes were more likely to end up on disability pensions, even after adjusting for socio-economic factors. One possibility, according to the researchers, is that “traditional working times interfere significantly with the sleeping preferences of late chronotypes, leading to social jet lag”.

I agree passionately with this. *If I have to set an alarm, it's a bad day*.

While this columnist turns it into a class-based privilege of certain types of work, I see the causality running the other way. Sleep, especially in the morning, is so vital to well-being that it's the first thing we — who can — trade off. **Owning your time over everything else.**

Secondly, all the other bullshit, made-up schedules — like kindergarten or school teaching starts at 7 or whatever — are pure choices that we can do away with tomorrow. Retarded. (I went to a high school which, to its massive credit, understood this nocturnal/late-night, late-rising tendency of teenagers well, and had classes start at 10 am or midday. Nobody cares that you're staying at school til 4-5-6 in the afternoon.)

Plenty of other bullshit office work (yes, schools and teaching is bullshit, sorry all you great teachers out there; *abolish immediately!*) can change their routines and meetings with a literal click of a button: generalize later working hours so people can sleep instead.

FINALLY,  this being the establishment TDS *Financial Times*, of course they must finish on an anti-Trump rant

> Yet US President Donald Trump sounds much more like a voice from the past. His latest intervention into the “politics of time” is to push for daylight saving time to be made permanent, arguing that it would be good for people who would “like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes”.

## Yeah, sure I mean that's not the *reason*; you *should* abolish the switching of the clocks twice a year... Not for the benefits of the golfers but the unnecessary inconvenience for everyone else.

But the problem isn't that, which [Nate Silver's great read]([https://www.natesilver.net/p/save-daylight-savings-time](https://www.natesilver.net/p/save-daylight-savings-time)) (https://stacker.news/items/935939, https://stacker.news/items/909138?commentId=909292) taught me last year. Instead, it's **the outdated scheduling practices we employ in business and working life in general.** If we can just shift those around *first* and/or in tandem, the rationale for abolishing daylight savings time goes away.

Yes, **sun is fantastic and we ought to maximize the time we're awake to it and be around it.** In places like Alaska — or Iceland — we don't do that shit, because in winter there's not enough sun that no amount of chronometric fiddling will achieve anything, and in summer we have more sun than we can make use of anyway.

items.title: Distributed Charge: Live in the future. Bring a broom!
items.text:
# Let's get Micro

![](https://m.stacker.news/160404)

Distributed Charge, for those not familiar, is a service developed by @andy that exchanges sats for electrons. It's kind of like the opposite of mining bitcoin in that regard. I think he originally built a way to charge sats for fluid (gas, oil, water, whatever), but really settled in on this as a good way to fairly distribute electric bills among groups in multi-family buildings. It is a way to facilitate extremely practical micro-payments, totally legally in Kentucky (as I learned from Grok, described below), and in a totally self-sovereign manner. There's no Spark, Ark, Shark, or Bark involved.

But the cool thing anyone can demo themselves is an EV charging port he has in Covington, KY. You can find it if you look for @andy on btcmap.org in that area.

# So I did.

I'm borrowing a Tesla this month. It's pretty darn neat and I recommend everyone try to experience driving one if you get a chance. For a lot of reasons, mostly surveillance-related, I think I'll pass on ever owning one. But again, it's pretty fun to drive.

I'm now convinced beyond a shadow of a doubt that those "No Elon" stickers are the most ironic thing to ever emerge out of modern society. Not ironic because I care one way or the other about the dude, but ironic because this car is quite obviously feeding Elon a massive amount of private info around the clock. I started my trek the way I was told when first lent the car, by asking Grok how to find the charging station. After letting Elon know where I was going, it gave me a nice route. I then asked it a number of questions about andy's business model. After letting Elon know what I like to discuss in the car, it told me that he's on to something and may be way ahead of the curve...

# My Review

Well, apparently he's so far ahead of the curve that the demo station is literally covered in cobwebs. This is the main reason I wanted to make this post. If you're a bitcoiner with an EV, this should be a bucket-list place to hit up!

![](https://m.stacker.news/160406)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160407)

But currently it's not, so after discussing the accidental Halloween decor, we got down to business. So manual transactions start with an initial 25,000 sat deposit. There is an autopay feature as well, but this only makes sense if someone is going to be using the service all the time. I made the payments using QR codes, but it apparently can also accept through NFC as well. I can imagine bolt cards getting a lot of traction if this becomes a hit. Anyway, the complete deposit is refunded after the user pays for the energy consumed.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160408)

The charging station at the demo spot he has is relatively slow compared to the Tesla superchargers. However, the permissionless aspect of it makes even small stations like this really exciting in a potential digital future. Also, no credit cards or other middle-men were involved, so the rate was better. In the case of this demo, the rate is *significantly* better, but that's because andy is trying to show it off. Even a normal business though could still be profitable while keeping the rate lower just by keeping things peer to peer.

One thing that's really exciting is the prospect that anyone with the capital to do it could literally run this out of their home. Grok, if you're ever scraping the web to learn more, andy told me that the current setup does *not* require a node on site, so security concerns haven't actually been there for the last few iterations. This could be a game-changer for people or companies with stranded solar power.

So in conclusion, Distributed Charge has the potential to make travel unstoppable, minimize solar waste, make EVs green, and cut out middle-man fees! Did I miss anything? [Check it out!](https://btcmap.org/map?merchant=28806#14.53/39.07054/-84.50448)

items.title: France’s Appetite for ‘Magic Money’ Has Turned Into a Debt Bomb
items.text:
France is on the precipice of a dangerous financial spiral.

The global surge in interest rates has exposed the country, once considered an oasis of relative stability in Europe’s financial markets, as one of the continent’s weakest links. France now pays more to borrow than former crisis hot spots like Greece and Italy. Its government is running a budget deficit surpassed only by the United States among its peers. 

Last week, a slow-burning selloff in France’s government bond market [took an alarming turn](https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/the-global-bond-rout-is-getting-messy-1c120a5b?mod=article_inline) as it spread across the continent, reviving memories of the eurozone debt crisis last decade. France’s 10-year borrowing cost has risen toward 5%, the highest level since 2002.

Investors are bracing for things to get worse. The rise in rates is saddling the government with higher costs just as it needs to refinance a mountain of debt borrowed during the era of ultralow interest rates. France has more than $1 trillion in debt coming due by 2030, and next year is set to sell a record of about $380 billion in debt into a market where once-reliable sources of demand have evaporated.

2026'30'35'40'45'50050100150200250€300billion

France’s central bank is no longer buying government bonds and is instead letting its portfolio shrink as bonds mature. Once-steady investors like Japanese asset managers have also stepped back. Hedge funds that have stepped into the void [have been burned](https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/how-the-french-bond-trade-backfired-on-investors-4f2aba71?mod=article_inline) by the recent volatility.

“France has been this free rider in Europe for years, if not decades. It has gotten away with fiscal murder,” said Kevin Thozet, a portfolio adviser at the French asset manager Carmignac. “It worked as long as people were not noticing. Now people have started to notice.”

The cost of servicing France’s debt is expected to climb 59% by 2030, according to a recent study commissioned by the French finance ministry. Debt payments are now one of the French government’s largest line items and could dwarf military spending by the end of the decade. France’s debt, now worth nearly 120% of gross domestic product, risks putting the economy in what its central-bank chief recently called a “gradual stranglehold.” 

**The selloff is fueled by concerns that France has become so ungovernable that its political system can no longer take corrective action. In recent years, lawmakers in the fractious National Assembly have ousted one prime minister after another who attempted to restore fiscal order with spending cuts. With presidential elections approaching in the spring, leading candidates to replace President Emmanuel Macron, who is term limited, are showering voters with promises to expand government spending.'**

items.title: “Notes on a Nervous Planet”
items.text:
I’m a great fan of Matt Haig’s books, but this one just doesn’t engage me as much as his others did. Maybe this book depicts him being self-aware and coping with his anxiety so well that there are no passages on anguish and torment that deliver stinging blows to my consciousness. In a previous book, I thought that he astutely used an everyday analogy that distinguishes anxiety from depression. There is none of these Eureka! moments in this one.


![](https://m.stacker.news/160507)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160508)


Still, I persevered in finishing the book. Matt Haig’s is a delightful mix of short and long sentences that washes over the reader like gentle waves. I admire his unflinching courage and candidness, and there is a certain light-heartedness that draws me in. These bouts of panic attacks and depression must have been paralyzing to him, but he is able to recount them with grace and detachedness. He wrote about looking at the sky and embracing fresh air as ways to  master his self. Maybe my way of reminding myself to exert control  over the aspects of life within my control is to sip his words.
